pointers.sentence: Django's `Index` names none, and gets a B-tree, which the documentation finds of little help with complex types: GiST may suit a range or an hstore, it says, and GIN an array (`docs/ref/contrib/postgres/fields.txt`).

An exclusion constraint forbids two rows for which every one of a list of comparisons, each with its own operator, is true; PostgreSQL implements it with an index (`docs/ref/contrib/postgres/constraints.txt`).

It calls `PostgresIndex.check_supported`, an empty hook no class here overrides; hands `Index.create_sql` a `"USING"` clause with the class's suffix, `"btree"` for `BTreeIndex`; and puts what `PostgresIndex.get_with_params` returns in a `"WITH"` clause after any `"INCLUDE"`, before a tablespace or a condition (`django/contrib/postgres/indexes.py:PostgresIndex.create_sql`).
Bloom is an extension, which the documentation says to install with `BloomExtension` (`docs/ref/contrib/postgres/indexes.txt`).

`PostgresIndex.max_name_length` is thirty less three plus the length of the class's suffix: an unnamed `SpGistIndex` on the sailings' window is named `"charts_sail_window_95d66d_spgist"`, 32 characters (`django/contrib/postgres/indexes.py:PostgresIndex.max_name_length`).
Over expressions, the expression is wrapped in `OpClass`, a `Func` that writes it and then the class's name (`django/contrib/postgres/indexes.py:OpClass`).

It lifts its wrapper classes off the top of the expression, puts the rest in parentheses unless it resolves to a column, and nests the wrappers back around it in the order of `IndexExpression.wrapper_classes`, the first outermost (`django/db/models/indexes.py:IndexExpression.resolve_expression`).

`PostgresConfig.ready` makes those `OrderBy`, `OpClass` and `Collate` with `IndexExpression.register_wrappers`, so that after an index's column come its collation, its operator class and its direction, in that order (`django/contrib/postgres/apps.py:PostgresConfig.ready`).

In `validate`, an exclusion or a unique constraint drops an `OpClass`, whose `OpClass.constraint_validation_compatible` is false, from the top of an expression: `BaseExpression.get_expression_for_validation` returns the expression inside, one level only (`django/db/models/expressions.py:BaseExpression.get_expression_for_validation`).

`ExclusionConstraint.__init__` checks the index type, the expressions' shape and the types of the condition, the deferrable and the include, and refuses a hash index with more than one pair, with an include, or with an operator other than `RangeOperators.EQUAL` (`django/contrib/postgres/constraints.py:ExclusionConstraint.__init__`).

`ExclusionConstraint.constraint_sql` compiles them and the condition as an index's are, without table names and with values written in by the editor's `quote_value`, and asks the editor for the `"INCLUDE"` and `"DEFERRABLE"` clauses (`django/contrib/postgres/constraints.py:ExclusionConstraint.constraint_sql`).
The documentation asks for the btree_gist extension with GiST (`docs/ref/contrib/postgres/constraints.txt`).
`ExclusionConstraint.validate` asks whether a stored row would break the rule with the instance (`django/contrib/postgres/constraints.py:ExclusionConstraint.validate`).
A condition goes through `Q.check`, which tests it on the instance's values together with an `Exists` of those rows that meet it (`django/db/models/query_utils.py:Q.check`).

And it works only on PostgreSQL, the one database for which `PostgresOperatorLookup` writes SQL (`django/db/models/lookups.py:PostgresOperatorLookup.as_postgresql`): on the harbour's SQLite database it raised `NotImplementedError`, "Subclasses must implement as_sql()".
